Theatre is a space for bold ideas—a shared experience that opens hearts, sparks thought, and pushes us to imagine a better world.

I played Cordelia opposite Christopher Plummer during the Stratford Festival’s 50th anniversary. That image became a poster sold in the giftshop—I still have one framed on my wall. Cordelia embodies fearless truth, speaking up no matter the cost.

That production nearly broke me. But the late Peter Donaldson reminded me: you’re doing your job—making people feel, think, and wake up. That’s what matters.

It’s taken years to understand: as actors, we’re meant to provoke, not please—and that has nothing to do with our worth.

Cordelia’s honesty drew me in from the start. It still feels like home.

I’ll be stepping into an expanded role beyond the stage soon—one rooted in making a difference. Theatre has shaped everything that’s led me here—stay tuned.
In the meantime: www.sarahmcvie.com

My friends! It’s been years of UPS, downs and all arounds. I consider this year official midlife because one grandparent lived to 95 so if I should be so lucky this is it! I have so many things I want to share (they’ve all been documented) so now I will work on perfecting my delivery for maximum delight and inspiration. In the meantime I’m getting back to the work I love most:acting. Come see me on stage @coalminetheatre in Eureka Day—All of February. And then come see me in a new play by George F. Walker called Syndrome produced by @theatredirect …it’s been 10 years since I was on stage which for this theatre kid makes no sense at all. Live theatre is my absolute passion. I can’t express how excited I am about this return to my roots as an actor. It comes after a few years of intense work on a very local issue in my community that has dominated my attention and time. Shout out to my family and friends for putting up with the obsession. Already we know it was worth the effort but I am grateful for everyone who put up with so many hours of talk about sewage and water infrastructure, economic and environmental racism, the illusion of a “polite society” in our beloved country and the hard work of countering the nastiness of slow violence and systemic neglect of marginalized communities. It wasn’t my sexiest conversation topics but you listened, supported me gave feedback that has helped lead me to…ugh I just go ON and ON so instead
Follow my other account @blackcreekfloodcoalition for more serious and worrisome content about the systematic slow violence done to the Toronto community where I landed in 2021. Others see the horror and move away (don’t blame them) but I decided to stay and document the clear neglect that has tormented my neighbours for decades. I’m not going to let it go until my community gets the protection and dignity everyone deserves. So ya. Follow that other account for those updates and follow this one for the acting stuff. I am so fucking grateful to be alive and have you willing to come along with me for this ride. I wish I could throw a HUGE party and all of you and everyone I have loved and lost and met and missed could be together. HappyNY!

LANDED IN SCHITT’S CREEK—for real you guys! 
In 2021, I found a home in York South–Weston. Amazing community. Incredible neighbours. Sewage in the basement when it rains. 🫠
Turns out we’ve been living in an ongoing infrastructure horror show —I’m new to the cast but let me tell you this gig doesn’t pay well at all! One of my neighbours has been reporting this issue to city officials since 1984—truly the stuff of nightmares! 🧟‍♂️
We’ve had floods, property damage, and broken promises from the folks elected to help. So we got organized. In January, a few of us started meeting. Now we’ve grown into the Black Creek Flood Coalition — and this week, we delivered 200+ petition signatures to City Hall.
Did our councillor show up? Nope. But they sent a staffer, and we dropped the other envelope, addressed to our Mayor, in the lobby mailbox. 📬
Big thanks to journalist Gabe Oatley at @torontotoday for covering our “Black Creek horror show.” Search his name + “Black Creek” if you want the tea.
We’re on Bluesky, Facebook, X, and Nextdoor. Not flooding this feed with sewage shots (you’re here for red carpets and butt-shaking content, I know🍑😘). But I wanted you to see this — because maybe you’ve got your own version of broken systems and crumbling infrastructure.
If so, may I recommend the #CoalitionLifestyle: meet your neighbours, demand better, and raise some polite but persistent hell. 💪🌊

Now she’s 20. Back then I yearned to be a mom but being an Auntie brought me so much joy it eased the longing. Now I make believe with my own bonus kid and find my feelings of wanting and lacking have almost entirely melted away. Things change. Time passes and when the root of the thing is honoured, in my case the desire to mother, to care for and to nurture, if that root is strong and holds you up in every moment then life has a way of leading you towards the very thing you desire. Acting and theatre have taught me to dream big and stay open to possibilities. The process of making art has informed my approach to life. It has taught me to appreciate all that feels good, even the tiny moments of play with a child I adore. This dual focus on a big picture and the everyday minutia can be exciting and exhausting at the same time. I can understand why some might find it’s easier to just tune out or numb any big or complex feelings or thoughts. It can all feel so overwhelming. I have tuned out and numbed my senses plenty of times and thankfully that habit didn’t stick in part because I had developed another habit: the habit of focusing my feelings into something creative. I’m drawn to the discomfort of big emotions and thoughts because I trained to live inside of it. If you are the guardian of a young person I urge you to get them involved in the arts. Find them good teachers with practical experience in whatever art form appeals: music, drama, painting, sculpting, writing and any other creative outlet available. That is how we find our inner strength and stand up for each other. It is the arts that give us our ability to communicate and make lasting social change. 

This little bee is studying psychology at uni. My little bee has his sights on ship design. I wanted to be a million different things and continue to stay open to what I might do in the years ahead. What a gift it is to be engaged with creativity, to think and see beyond what is being sold, proclaimed or touted as fact. We create our world. We all need to be creative. The importance of an arts education can’t be minimized in a society that struggles to honour the value of humanity.🎨❤️💙💜🖤💛💚

I’m really grateful that you continue to follow me, even though I haven’t had much professional acting content to share lately. I lost a few followers recently and wondered if it’s because I am “this” or “that”. The thing I know is it doesn’t really matter. I’ve had lots of people come and go throughout my life: friends, acquaintances, lovers etc.— and that’s ok. I have trained myself not to take it personally and hope others can do the same. That said I’m sure glad I’m at a point in my life where I have the confidence to handle rejection and not let it hurt me or make me sad. I worry about those who aren’t as practiced in the art of constant and blatant rejection. One of the upsides of being an actor—the resilience we require to survive in an industry that won’t coddle you one tiny bit! It can be brutal! 😁

Anyways, I asked Rui to take these pictures of me at the beach last week because I was feeling so f-ing great. I used to have such awful thoughts about myself and especially about my body. The searing monthly endometriosis pain from age 11 onwards didn’t help things. Neither did the messaging from our sick beauty obsessed culture. So having done so much work over the years (thank god for therapy and others who demonstrate body confidence and reject those dangerous and narrow ideas of a standard of beauty!!!🙏) that now that I’m enjoying the fruits of my labour—feeling awesome in my own skin—I feel compelled to share my success. Hence these very deliberate lifestyle pics! 

How you feel is everything! Work on feeling good now and the rest will fall into place I promise! That’s it, that’s all for now. That’s my hole story! 😉(It’s a visual pun because the pictures feature me with and around and in a bunch of holes—jokes are best when they need explaining!)

Found this lovely dress in a second hand shop years ago, long before I thought much about Portugal or her people. A time when I thought if I couldn’t have a child of my own I’d never be truly happy. In the middle of a painful stretch my mother gave me the best advice: try Sarah, try your best, but if it doesn’t happen don’t let it ruin your life. 

Even before that, during a difficult crisis, a gifted counsellor, seeing the need to nurture in me, offered me a way to think that got me though dark times: be your own mother. Care for yourself like you are your own beloved child. 

These bits of wisdom take time to sink in. I’m glad I bought the dress before I had the opportunity to wear it. I was ready for this moment even if I couldn’t see it coming.

Happy Spring Equinox my friends! 🌷Tomorrow I flow into the second half of my little life (should I be lucky enough to live roughly as long as the average age of my grandparents!). Val might call this birthday “the big BIGGER BIGGEST ONE!” 🎉
 
I’m thankful and hopeful I’ll live to see the mass epidemic of loving kindness I fantasize about before my time is up. I know—seems unlikely given the horrific and scary things happening but here’s the thing—I’ve personally experienced such marvellous mysterious unexpected and RADICAL change in my own life that after years of suffering and searching and hoping and growing I have come to feel something that is best described as faith. No, I’m not starting a cult (though I do think I’d make an excellent leader of one!). 
I’ve shared publicly my struggles with conditions like endometriosis, depression, psoriasis and the even more evil incarnation psoriatic arthritis — it’s a lot and isn’t even the full picture. Bottom line is: chronic pain has been a constant. In those long hours/days/months of pain, I’d sometimes feel hopeless. Solutions might work for a time, but the pain would always come back. A few years ago, at a low point, I finally took my mom’s advice and tried what she calls praying—which could also be called meditating. It gave me an incredible sense of calm and what I now refer to as faith. This habit of tuning in to my inner being, energizing thoughts of joy and pleasure while letting go of negativity has brought about a life changing shift towards real mental wellness. We all know the importance of our brains. There is lots of science to support this idea of positive thinking. I’m not talking about toxic positivity here—I’m talking about constructive, purposeful, focused thinking. For years I’ve made vision boards and no I didn’t get all the things I’d pasted on there — but when I look back I see that I kept my intentions clear and I now enjoy versions of all of it. Buddha put it best: “All that we are is the result of what we have thought” My birthday wish for you my friends is that you find peace and pleasure as you navigate the intensity of life using the power of your mighty and mysterious brain. 🧠 💜

Happy New Year my Friends! 🥳🥳🥳
Some of you may have noticed I’ve been off social media for a while. I don’t have to tell you how tricky it can feel to share personal content in a public space with so much going on in our complex world. I’ve been analyzing my reticence to share (there was a time I was posting stories daily) and I’ve been carefully considering what it does to me when I contain myself and I have to tell you it doesn’t feel great. What got me so clammed up? 🧐 I’m even more perplexed how I have amassed such an impressive group of people (you!) who have chosen to “Follow” me, some of you for years now, only to withdraw into my shell, hiding my unique brand of zany from my audience? 🐢 Maybe it was partly because this year my decades long dream to became a real (bonus/step) MOM came true and I love the experience even more than I imagined I would. Or perhaps I felt inspired not to post content in a time when I wanted to show solidarity with my colleagues in the biz who took critical and costly job actions for our greater good. For sure there are lots of possible reasons and I don’t regret anything; it’s been a time of contemplation and I value the experience. But I have to be honest with you, it’s mostly been fear keeping me quiet. How could I possibly say anything worthwhile? What could I say or do that would contribute the good I want to add to a world full of pain and in need of deep healing? Who wants to hear from me right now? I wasn’t sure and I was fixated on the doubt I had something of value to offer.
Well that was last year.
After lots of work to get myself into a place of good health, meaningful connection (with immediate friends, family, neighbours) and now operating with that ultimate vibration — JOY! — I’ve decided to get back on the “saddle” and do the thing I have always loved most - entertain people. 😁
So my friends — thank you for sticking around. I’ve missed interacting with you and I hope to give you amusing and thought-provoking content that tickles your fancy in 2024 and beyond! 💖

She knows very well how happy I am these days because she’s seen me struggle to connect with the right romantic partner for many, many years. I’ve wanted to be an actor since before I can remember. It was always my passion and plan. Marriage never held much interest to me. I didn’t dream about my wedding or the white dress. I wasn’t one of those kids who carries a doll and pretends it’s a baby. But at age 20 I developed a deep desire to be a mom. I became fixated on the idea and was consciously looking everywhere for the right man. I had many wonderful romances, but never the one. A few friends volunteered to donate to the cause but it didn’t work out. One heartbreaking miscarriage led me to believe it was possible and so I decided to go it alone. It took years of saving to have the funds to try a round of IVF that sadly didn’t come to fruition. The dream I’d been pursuing for decades was dead. I mourned. I got very sad. I had A LOT of help to move through the grief. I’d just purchased a house intended to be the perfect space to foster new life. My mother and sister dropped everything and drove the 5 hours to be at my side. Natural caregivers, they arrived with armfuls of food and immediately set about weeding my lawn and washing my windows. They listened to me talk and wail and they wept with me. My sister, a brilliant counsellor, knew that making a plan for the road forward would help me heal. It sure did. A year later I fell in love with a marvellous man who lives up the street. Someone I would never have crossed paths with had it not been for my buying this house far from my usual stomping grounds, purchased for a different purpose but now reimagined and full of joyous gathering, friendship and love. My bf has two lovely boys who I adore. They get on super well with my 3 nieces. I have lots of young people in my life through friends, colleagues, community groups and daily park walks. These days life is grand and I don’t take any of it for granted. I share this for anyone who is feeling low and in need of a reminder that while our dreams might not come true, something else, something equally as marvellous and fulfilling can happen. 
To my fellow women for whom Mother’s Day is hard-I see you. I encourage you to care for yourself as you would’ve cared for that lucky child who would call you mom.❤️

Today’s post is an ode to the awesome experience of being in so many group scenes with so many women over the years. 

My early years acting professionally were spent on stage at the Stratford Festival of Canada-a prestigious classical theatre company that centres on the works of William Shakespeare. I was an apprentice actor in 2001 and the company was predominantly male, because the roles are overwhelmingly male in those plays and in those days there wasn’t much cross casting, certainly not in the big parts. I have a distinct memory of the first table read for Henry the Fourth-scanning the huge circle of actors and counting 20+ men compared to us 5 women in the cast. It was the norm at the time, but I remember clocking it and wondering if things would change in my lifetime.

Over the years things did change, of course. 

Then eventually along came Workin’ Moms! 

Those early days of shooting season one felt surreal at times. To sit in a circle with all these talented, funny female artists, to have the brave female creator encouraging me to let loose in this zany role, saying things I hadn’t heard women say on tv at that point, surrounded by women in key crew positions, getting alt lines flown in from the team of hilarious female writers, it was such a new feeling-the experience of being inside something that was created with a female gaze. Heaven. Seven years. So many circles. It’s been a treat. ⭕️❤️

Honoured to be nominated for Best Supporting Performer, Comedy alongside cast mate Enuka Okuma and 6 other phenomenal artists who I admire. Catherine and Dani are nominated in the lead category and Workin’ Moms has 8 nominations overall including best writing, direction, photography and editing. 

The Canadian Screen Awards are our equivalent of the Oscars and Emmys in the US, or the BAFTAs in the UK or Goyas in Spain. They recognize technical and artistic achievement in film, television and digital media. Members of the Academy of Canadian Cinema and Television vote on submissions and then a small group meet and discuss who should make the final cut to nominee. Then voting opens up again to the wider membership and winners are announced at ceremonies that take place in Toronto during April. 🤩
The Academy has done away with gender specific categories for acting, meaning the only consideration is the work of each actor within a genre (comedy, drama, film, tv etc.) and separated into role categories (lead, supporting, guest star). I applaud this change and I’m thrilled to be included as a nominee in this first year of gender neutral performer categories.

Happy Birthday to a canine icon! 🐩🤩💫🎉9 years of bliss with my baby girl. 🥰If you’ve had the pleasure of meeting Coco, or perhaps have followed us on social, you know how special she is. A #Queen who loves the comfort of a soft, plushy, clean surface but can also get down and #dirty in the mud. The dog of my dreams. Best decision I ever made! 

I’ll share my favourite early Coco memory. We were out in the Okanagan working at The Caravan Farm Theatre (check it out, a true cultural gem of Canadian Theatre) and the living out there was rough and tumble compared to what we were used to in Toronto’s #QueenWest. Coyotes would try to lure Coco all the time. Big farm dogs from around would come visit and put my little princess through a toughness test that she passed, but only after shaving a few years off of this nervous new dog mama’s life. At one year old my little pup had suddenly gone from city living to country life. That summer was incredible for both of us. Hanging with awesome people in Armstrong and floating down the Shuswap river on our days off. Coco took it all like a champ. One night when the party had gone late and I was the last to head for my little cabin, I stopped for a pee in a field, with the full moon glowing over head. I took in the beauty of the place, the people, the work, the moment I found myself blessed to have encountered and in my reverie I turned to see my little angel, a few feet from me, facing the same direction like a mirror image, peeing in unison, looking right at me. Who knows what she was thinking, but my god I felt a bond with her in that moment that has never left us. I cherish each moment I get with this beautiful soul. What a gift to know such profound connection and deep deep love. ❤️

It’s World Theatre Day! 🎭
I have tickets for upcoming Toronto productions and I’m excited to see theatre again and frankly I’d love to DO a piece of theatre again. The last time I “trod the boards” was in a play I co-created called The Public Servant (I hope this play will have another life as it’s themes are timely and it’s a total crowd pleaser) I’ve loved performing from the time I started walking. When I struggled in my early teens I found pleasure in escaping into imagined circumstances. My parents recognized a serious passion and enrolled me in classes at the newly founded Ottawa School of Speech and Drama. The founder of OSSD, Natalie Stern, asked me why I wanted to be an actor. My mother recently re-told me this story; I remember the meeting with Natalie but no details beyond Ms. Stern’s fire red hair and commanding presence in the old Atelier studio space on King Edward Drive. According to my mother, my response to the question “why an actor?” was “I want to make people think.” 
My experience of participating in theatre has been an ongoing process of learning new perspectives on everything. When I engage with a piece of theatre I feel such a tremendous thrill to be sharing time and space with other people as we contemplate what is unfolding in front of us as a collective. After the show we might debate the content of the play but the act of witnessing together has made a path for us to safely exist in our disagreements or discomforts. It offers us a way to connect and celebrate this mystery that is life on planet earth. Theatre has given me a tremendous sense of belonging and I am forever in its debt. 

HAPPY #WORLDTHEATREDAY!

I’d like to bring some awareness to a condition called #Endometriosis. It affects at least 1 in 10 people with a uterus. Cells similar to uterus cells will grow outside the uterus so that during your period, these lesions will bleed with no route out of the body. This leads to scarring and in some cases severe pain and other horrible symptoms like vomiting and infertility. I hope if you are suffering there is a solution within reach. Don’t give up! Science is amazing! Research is being done especially now that women are in those top doc positions! I hope I live long enough to see real options for everyone who suffer from this debilitating disease. 

@endocanada @endonetwork_canada
#endometriosisawarenessmonth 

I’d like to add a personal note about my own experience of this disease and a recent treatment that seems to work. ENDOMETRIOSIS has caused me a great deal of pain for 3+ decades. I was diagnosed at 23 after years debilitating pain and dark days spent doubled over. Words like gruelling, unrelenting, searing, sharp, vomit-inducing and demoralizing come to mind. Dealing with this pain has been the predominant challenge in my life. I’ve had a lot of support in my journey and a huge reason I’ve survived and even thrived despite my disability is because of my privileged circumstances. Many therapies have helped support my mental health as I navigated the unpredictable and punishing bouts of pain. At one point in my 20’s I was prescribed oxy and luckily for me it made me 🤢 so I stopped using it. Pot has been helpful but often the pain was too much. 
After closing the door on fertility last year, I decided to try an IUD to end my endo pain. It was painful for a few weeks but for the past three months I’ve had no pain at all.🤞This is just my experience. More research and understanding of the disease will hopefully bring more and better alternatives. 
Love to all! 💃🏝❤️

Read more: warning-long post, body image issues, white privilege
Body confidence has been a struggle for me. I’ve posted before about being teased about my size, that was the most obvious source of pain for many years. I also took a lot of flack about my “boy voice.” There are other things too, of course. I don’t remember being teased about my freckles, and often got compliments from boys when they got to see them up close. 
I do remember reading about how to cover up/reduce/eliminate freckles in teen magazines and taking from those articles the notion that freckles were not good. Fast forward to my adult years, even after a lot of work to nurture strong self acceptance, I found myself approaching middle age and falling prey to messages that my beauty was in decline. I began contemplating treatments to enhance my attractiveness. While getting a routine facial at a spa I saw an ad for laser treatments that reduce sun damage. I inquired and was told it would not only reduce spots but in fact eliminate my freckles. At first I was taken back, but then I considered the idea. I left that day with a seed that had been planted many years ago, sprouting a fresh root in my brain. 
Months later, back for another routine facial, I asked more questions about the laser thing and was shown some before and after pics. Still not ready to commit, I left with the pricing info. Later that day my sister texted me. My youngest niece, then 9 years old, had done an assignment for school about her favorite body part. What do you think she chose? I am forever grateful to the universe for these timely messages. I’m thankful for the ability to see the error of my ways and the capacity to shift my thinking and change. 
I’m lucky to have a close relationship with three wonderful young women who constantly remind their Auntie Sarah what true beauty is.

My maternal grandmother, Grace Cullen (née Taylor), born in 1907. Grace graduated in 1931 from Queen’s University and worked as a teacher in a one room schoolhouse in Eganville, Ontario before she began a career at External Affairs Canada. When she married my grandfather, William Cullen in 1947, she resigned from her professional work because that was what was expected of women in those days. Shortly thereafter, at age 41, she gave birth to my mother. My Aunt came two years later. Grace worried she wouldn’t live long enough to hear me speak, but she did. In fact she lived with us for much of my childhood and was fondly known as Nanny. Alzeihmer’s disease slowly and cruelly stole this intelligent, strong and dignified woman from us too soon. Thankfully I have many fond memories of those years she lived with us and the fantastical imaginings Grace would have (a result of her illness), transporting her to far off places, my sister and I following right along, just the right age to embrace imaginative play and remain non-judgemental about the fact that our Nanny was now referring to us by names we didn’t recognize but that we took on without hesitation. I sometimes wonder if these early experiences with Grace had something to do with my pursuing acting as a passion and (lucky me) a career.

I am forever inspired by this amazing women. One of many remarkable women I admire and appreciate today and every day.

In 2007 I bought a house. I got a loan because I’d been working at a gym as a trainer, though my down payment was saved up from five years working at a large theatre (banks look poorly on an actors salary). It was a struggle to maintain at various times, and when my income couldn’t cover the bills I would either rent the second bedroom or move out temporarily and live with family. Everyone who rented over the years expressed what a great house it is. Good vibes. It became vacant a few months ago so I moved back in. The old ghosts were all there and in fine form. 👻🥂 Lisa (dear friend/one time roommate/neighbour) and her pup Winnie were close by and my goodness it feels nice to have friends in similar boats (single/dogmamas who like hot men and cold wine). Distance hang outs ensued. Walks to our favourite (Reid) park resumed. But in the end I didn’t have the $ to do the renovations a 100+ house deserves. And banks still don’t appreciate my acting income (it’s lower than you think). So I sold the house. The first day I saw it I had envisioned raising a child inside it. That never happened. Almost happened once, but then it didn’t. I have wanted to be a mother for a long time and no doubt I’ve had some fun trying along the way 😉 but ultimately my “dream” didn’t materialize. Instead I’ve spent over a decade having the most incredible adventures with so many fabulous people, working consistently in theatre and now television, teaching all kinds of things to all ages and learning useful skills like how to caulk and plunge, level and lay flagstone. I don’t have a family yet and who knows what the future holds, but what I’ve learned from this experience owning a house is that a material thing serves us if it doesn’t force us to remain held to preconceived ideas about ourselves and what makes for a meaningful and enjoyable life.

It’s National Canadian Film Day and there is so much incredible Canadian cinema to celebrate! 
I have many favourites but Atom Egoyan’s The Sweet Hereafter is one of the most memorable film experiences I’ve had in my life. I was nearing the end of high school when this exceptionally crafted film challenged my understanding of the complexity of human relationships. I was transported by the storytelling to such an extent that I felt uncomfortable watching parts of the film. If you haven’t seen it I warn you the subject matter could be triggering. I love comedy (obviously) but sometimes I crave a dark and disturbing drama to help me contemplate the ugly part of human nature. This movie is one of the most breathtakingly beautiful and challenging dramas I’ve ever seen. It’s a powerful film and one of many gems in our Canadian canon. 
Reel Canada is the non-profit organization that hosts National Canadian Film Day as part of their work to promote our rich inventory of diverse Canadian films. They have curated a list of “20+20” Canadian Films available for streaming through a link on their website canadianfilmday.ca

They are also presenting a Livestream tonight from 6-10PM EDT,  featuring talent like Sandra Oh, Colm Feore, Meghan Follows and #WorkinMoms own Peter Keleghan to name a few. 
You can also stream over 120 Canadian Films anytime on the FREE app CBC GEM. (I pay the 5$/month for ad free)

I wish you all a great day and hope you’ll join me in celebrating our cinematic culture by posting about the Canadian films you love!

It’s World Theatre Day. This image is from the Nightwood Theatre run of The Public Servant in Toronto in the winter of 2016. The show was commissioned and produced by Common Boots Theatre (formally Theatre Columbus) and was created by four women: Jennifer Brewin, Haley McGee, Amy Rutherford and myself. The production was supported by dozens more people who told us their stories, gave us their expertise, offered their time and donated their money to help make this work come to life. The show portrays work in the Canadian public service and examines the role non-elected government officials play in forming policies in a democratic society. We had two sold out runs and the reaction from the audience each night was thrilling. It will forever be a career highlight.
I believe the shared lived experience can never be replaced and will always have essential value to us. We will find our way through this current health crisis and as we do, we must remember that these things we took for granted, like gathering for a live show, are in fact sacred. 
On this particular World Theatre Day my thoughts are with my colleagues all over the world who have lost paid work for the time being. Stay strong and healthy my friends; we have much work to do to tell stories that will illuminate truths, entertain the masses and provoke meaningful discourse as we move into a brave new world post pandemic. #worldtheatreday #publicservantplay

When the Church we had been attending wouldn’t allow gay people to be married or serve in the ministry, we stopped going. So instead we would create our own little events full of costumes and pageantry in our house on Sunday mornings, or other times too. It was a time of galvanizing as a family, around what we stood for, what we believe to be important. I am ever grateful to my parents for instilling in me the values of compassion and inclusivity they share. We eventually returned to that Church when they finally came to their senses and changed the policies that were not in line with the beliefs they professed of unconditional love. I think of all you families who are isolated together right now and the wonderful opportunity to create rituals and pageants of your own. My favourite make shift costume always centered on a bed sheet and a belt. Come to think of it I might have to re-visit that look over the coming days. Sending love, light and the spirit of creativity from my bunker to yours.

My grandfather William Cullen was working for Canadian Foreign Affairs when he met my grandmother Grace Taylor who was then the administrative assistant to Prime Minister Lester B. Pearson. Fun fact: she was also one of the first women to graduate from Queen’s University. Grace stopped working when they married because that was expected in the 1940’s. The couple left Canada to fulfill William’s duties as Canadian consulate in Washington, then San Francisco and finally Los Angeles. My mother and aunt attended West Beverly High School in the 1960’s, a fact I always thought very cool, especially as a fan of the tv show Beverly Hills, 90210 in my teens. Recently my mom shared my grandfather’s scrapbook and I learned that he had been terrified of public speaking. William’s fear of speaking in front of others had been so debilitating that he dropped out of high school in his freshman year to avoid doing an oral presentation. He explains in the intro to his scrap book that he was successful in overcoming his fear (he calls it “abnormal” but we all know public speaking is one of the most common fears and most of us can relate to the terror it can inspire) and went on to give lots of talks and presentations and documented many of them in his scrapbook. It’s neat to be visiting Los Angeles this week and remember my incredible Grandfather who passed away 34 years ago tomorrow, and who I remember fondly but wish I’d had an opportunity to know better. I would love to ask him all about his fascinating life and career. I share these images in celebration of overcoming our fears and also in recognition of the good work members of the Canadian foreign service (including their spouses who contribute greatly to that work) have done to form positive relationships with countries all over the world.

Flashback Friday to my sexy pirate days. Truthfully I remember this time, those ripped jean shorts, that off-the-shoulder blouze…I remember loving the look, but feeling like absolute shit inside. Just hating my body, having internalized the names I was called in the schoolyard. In those days, the ones of this picture, the nick names were Tank, Miss Piggy and Elephant. What the fuck is wrong with people? A big question with no easy answer. I post this today because I had a conversation with a young person yesterday who is feeling the same way I did back then, about her own body; her beautiful, beautiful, unique and wonderful being. I wish I could take away her feelings of inadequacy, of being judged, take away her internalizing of the insults. I know from my own journey I can’t do the job, she will have a long road like I did to do the work it takes to heal. To all my brothers and sisters out there who are internalizing the hate: work to change the dialogue in your head. Invest time in carefully crafting the way you talk about yourself because you’re beautiful and one day you may look back and say goddamnit I was no tank, I was a sexy, vivacious, kind and fun loving pirate! Sending strength to all of you in the struggle to love yourself. I love every cell of you. Thank goodness we don’t all look alike: what a boring world it would be.

Coco was a sudden choice. I wanted a baby and that wasn’t happening so I got a furry place holder in exactly the right size. Dog Lady is inspired by my experience of being a human woman in these digital times. It’s about the pursuit of love, health, family, wealth, community and pleasure. My struggles with depression and addiction and pain have fuelled my desire to connect with others and tell stories and understand better and make people laugh, cry and feel things. Life is so complicated and rich, but at times it’s been nearly impossible to get out of bed. I’m fortunate in family and friends, but nothing compares to the incredible joy Coco has brought to my life. I used to swipe left on men with dogs, was worried about getting hair up my nose and everywhere else. Now I feel connected to every dog I meet. And the humans too. We are still animals and it’s okay to get dirty sometimes. I hope you like the trailer, Sam and I have lots of material ready to go so the more views it gets the closer we come to making a full series. Please share the link if you’re feeling it. 💗

Now, she’s a 20-year-old student who rises at dawn for Saturday yoga class and argues about the benefits and dangers of social media during debate night at @aunigeria. Today, Hauwa and more than 100 of her fellow students live on a pristine university campus 4 hours from their homes in northeastern Nigeria, their days filled with math and English classes and movie nights with popcorn. “I’m happy,” said Hauwa, who was No. 169 on a list of the missing girls. “But I’m thinking about my sisters who are still in the back,” in Boko Haram’s clutches, she said. Nigeria is in its 9th year of war with Boko Haram. Most victims will remain anonymous and unaccounted for. But the Chibok girls had names — and the world responded: #BringBackOurGirls.
